annotations.annotation_text: Celtic/mythological figure "Patrick" on page 491 ("The Inquest of Yawn"): invoking the ancient Fianna cycle and early Irish Christianity within the judicial inquest over the prostrate body of Yawn (Shaun), voices of the dead rising through him, HCE's final confession. During the Age of Men phase, this mythic presence grounds the universal dream in Ireland's heroic past, linking Finn MacCool's giant body to the Dublin landscape.
sources: MacKillop, James. Dictionary of Celtic Mythology. https://www.oxfordreference.com
Lady Gregory. Gods and Fighting Men. https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/14465
O'Hehir, Brendan. A Gaelic Lexicon for Finnegans Wake. https://archive.org/details/gaeliclexiconfor0000oheh

annotations.annotation_text: Viconian marker "Thunder" on page 491 ("The Inquest of Yawn"): Giambattista Vico's cyclical philosophy — divine, heroic, and human ages followed by thundering ricorso — structures this passage within the judicial inquest over the prostrate body of Yawn (Shaun), voices of the dead rising through him, HCE's final confession. The current Age of Men phase shapes the language, institutional imagery, and historical echoes of the dream.
sources: Beckett, Samuel. Dante... Bruno. Vico.. Joyce. https://archive.org/details/ourexagminationr0000unse
